extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and regulatory practitioners/commenters involved in rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and writing public comments for administrative rulemaking, with emphasis on persuasive content that influences agency decisionmaking. Focuses on informational versus threat-based tactics and what makes comments effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for informational persuasion over threats
rubrics_metrics.description: Two persuasion tactics in comments: informational (description of policy consequences) and threat (implicit/explicit warning of judicial review, congressional pressure, or political consequences). The vast majority of effective comments use informational tactics; threats are limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical finding: informational content predominates among effective comments. Strategic actors—even sophisticated ones—emphasize information over threats, suggesting agencies respond to information-based persuasion. Use threats sparingly and only in conjunction with substantive information establishing credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe specific policy consequences (not just preferences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comments 'describe what will happen' if the rule is adopted as proposed rather than merely stating preferences or objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete statements about consequences of the rule (operational impacts, downstream effects). Specificity builds credibility and makes it easier for agencies to incorporate the comment into rulemaking records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify impacts (costs, benefits, affected populations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should quantify impacts such as costs and benefits and identify which populations, firm sizes, sectors, or geographies are affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include cost figures grounded in specific operational analysis; provide quantified compliance burden broken out by firm size, sector, or geography; supply numerical estimates or ranges when possible to strengthen persuasive weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict behavioral responses by regulated parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comments predict how regulated parties will actually behave in response to the rule (e.g., compliance choices, adaptations, circumvention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain expected behavioral responses and link them to the rule's incentives or constraints. Showing predicted responses helps agencies assess real-world consequences beyond theoretical preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide credible factual basis before referencing judicial or political consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: If a comment references legal or political risks (litigation, congressional action), it should first present credible factual information that establishes the commenter's credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit or explicit threats are rarely persuasive on their own. An 'implicit threat works better when it follows substantive content'—so place factual evidence, analysis, and quantification before any mention of legal/political pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use legal/political threats only as supporting context, not primary persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: When raising legal or political risk, do so as supporting context rather than the primary mechanism for persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using threats as the central argument. If invoking judicial or congressional consequences, tie them to the substantive informational claims (e.g., show that a legal deficiency arises from the rule's factual effects) so the threat functions as corroborating context.
